Aldrich-McKelvey scaling

Source: R/svt.R
amscal.Rd

Recovers the positions of stimuli (parties, candidates, courts) on one scale from respondents' placements of them, each respondent allowed an own shift and stretch of the scale: \(z_{ij} = a_i + b_i \hat z_j + \epsilon_{ij}\). The positions are the least-squares solution of Aldrich and McKelvey (1977): with \(X_i = [1, z_i]\) and \(P_i\) the projection onto its columns, \(\hat z\) is the eigenvector of \(\sum_i (I - P_i)\) with the smallest eigenvalue orthogonal to the constant. Respondents with a missing placement, or who place every stimulus at the same point, are left out of that sum. The positions are standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, the first stimulus on the left. The respondent intercepts and slopes are each respondent's least-squares regression of the placements on those positions (defined with two placements or more; a slope of zero is set to 1e-10).

Usage

amscal(Z)

Arguments

Z

A respondent-by-stimulus matrix of placements, NA for a missing one.

Value

A list of class amscal: zhat (stimulus positions), alpha and beta (each respondent's intercept and slope) and weights (\(|b_i|\) scaled to sum to the number of respondents).

References

Aldrich, J. H. and McKelvey, R. D. (1977). A method of scaling with applications to the 1968 and 1972 presidential elections. American Political Science Review, 71(1), 111-130. doi:10.2307/1956957

Poole, K. T. (1998). Recovering a basic space from a set of issue scales. American Journal of Political Science, 42(3), 954-993. doi:10.2307/2991737

See also

Other scaling: anchv(), anomin(), bamscl(), bbscal(), bmdsf(), bunfld(), cjrirt(), cmdsf(), cutlns(), dblctr(), dwnom(), dynirt(), indscl(), ipsrec(), irtem(), irtlik(), irtpst(), mdsfit(), mlsmu(), nmdsf(), nombt(), nomll(), nompr(), nomutl(), nrmvec(), optcls(), ordirt(), ordocl(), procrs(), scboot(), smacf(), smunf(), unfstr(), votagr(), wrdfsh()

Examples

# 40 simulated respondents place five stimuli on a 1-7 scale
set.seed(1)
truth <- c(-1.2, -0.4, 0.1, 0.9, 1.5)
Z <- t(vapply(1:40, function(i) {
  4 + rnorm(1, 0, 0.3) + runif(1, 0.6, 1.4) * truth + rnorm(5, 0, 0.3)
}, numeric(5)))
round(amscal(Z)$zhat, 2)
#> [1] -1.28 -0.59 -0.05  0.67  1.25
round((truth - mean(truth)) / sd(truth), 2)
#> [1] -1.30 -0.55 -0.08  0.68  1.24
